Match scouting is the Scout-Ops Android app in `scouting/android`. A new question touches three layers:

1. The page (UI). Pick the phase in `scouting/android/lib/Match_Pages/match/`: `Auton.dart`, `TeleOperated.dart` or `EndGame.dart`. Each page follows the same pattern: a state variable, loaded in initState(), saved in UpdateData(), and a widget in build(). Reusable widgets are in `lib/components/` (e.g. buildCounter in `CounterShelf.dart`, buildCheckBox in `CheckBox.dart`).

2. The data class. In `lib/services/DataBase.dart` add the field to AutonPoints, TeleOpPoints or EndPoints: constructor, toJson, fromJson and toCsv. The compiler will then point you at the other places that build that class.

3. Downstream. The QR code is just MatchRecord.toCsv(), so column order matters. Whatever reads it has to learn the new column: the scanner app (`scouting/scan/lib/services/scout_ops_service.dart` and `neon_database.dart`) and the direct upload in `scouting/android/lib/services/NeonMatchService.dart`.

Here's the path an endgame field takes, in order:

1. UI: `scouting/android/lib/Match_Pages/match/EndGame.dart`. Add a state variable, load it in initState(), save it in UpdateData(), add the widget in build().
2. Data class: EndPoints in `scouting/android/lib/services/DataBase.dart`. Add it to the constructor, toJson, fromJson and toCsv (the compiler will flag the other places that construct EndPoints).
3. QR code: nothing to change. `components/QrGenerator.dart` just compresses MatchRecord.toCsv(), which ends with endPoints.toCsv().
4. Scanner app: `scouting/scan/lib/services/scout_ops_service.dart` has csvHeaders, and `scouting/scan/lib/services/neon_database.dart` has the CREATE TABLE in ensureTable() plus the columns list and INSERT in insertRecords().
5. Direct upload from the tablet: `scouting/android/lib/services/NeonMatchService.dart` has its own CREATE TABLE and INSERT, and reads values by toJson key.

Two things that bite people:
- The scanner matches CSV values to columns by position only. The order in toCsv, csvHeaders and the columns list must be identical, and the scanner's list ends with id, so your new column has to sit in the same spot everywhere.
- Both apps use CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS, so a table that already exists in Neon will not get the new column by itself. Ask your scouting lead how they want the existing table updated.

Want to start with step 1? What kind of question is it: counter, checkbox or text?

hint_corrections: scan/lib/models/scout_ops_data.dart does NOT need to change: ScoutOpsData keeps scanned rows as raw CSV strings and only reads columns 2, 4, 6, 7 (match number, alliance, station, battery). An endgame field comes after those.

toCsv() is defined in DataBase.dart (MatchRecord.toCsv -> EndPoints.toCsv); QrGenerator.dart only calls it and gzip+base64 encodes the result, so QrGenerator needs no edit. The scanner decodes base64+gzip in updateLastScan.

Scanner mapping is purely positional: insertRecords() maps CSV index i to columns[i]; csvHeaders is only used for the CSV export header (it is passed to insertRecords but unused). The list in neon_database.dart is what decides DB columns.

The android CSV has no Id value (it ends with the quoted Comments), while the scanner's csvHeaders/columns end with Id/id (filled with ''). A field appended after Comments in toCsv would land in the id column unless the scanner lists are updated in the same position.

Both CREATE TABLE statements are IF NOT EXISTS, so existing Neon tables do not gain the column automatically; the INSERT would then fail (the scanner swallows the error per record and reports 0 inserted).

NeonMatchService reads from record.toJson() by key (e.g. end['robotBroken']), not from the CSV, with numbered placeholders ($1..$30), so the toJson key name and placeholder count matter there rather than CSV order. Its table is '<eventKey>_match_scouting'; the scanner's table name comes from NeonConfig.
Also affected: match_page.dart:816 default EndPoints(...) and LocalDataBase.mapToEndPoints (positional constructor), android/test/match_data_generator_test.dart header string, android/Scouting.md.

Yes, that's G420 (TOWER protection). During the last 30 seconds of the match (END GAME), your robot can't contact an opponent robot that is touching its own TOWER. It counts whether the contact is direct or through a FUEL you're both touching, and it doesn't matter who started the contact.

Penalty: MAJOR FOUL (15 points to the other alliance), and if that robot is off the ground it is also awarded LEVEL 3 TOWER points (30 points).

So in END GAME, give robots at the opponent's TOWER a wide berth.

Yep, the math lives in one file:
`robot/2026-rebuilt/src/main/java/frc/robot/utils/ShootOnTheMove.java`

It computes a "virtual goal": the hub (or passing target) shifted backwards by the shooter's velocity times the ball's flight time, so the robot aims at where it needs to shoot while moving. The public entry points are `calculateVirtualGoalForShooting`, `calculateVirtualGoalForPassing` and `calculateRobotHeading`.

Where it's used:
- `commands/swerve/HubDrive.java`, `HubDriveAUTO.java` and the HUBDRIVE case in `TeleopSwerve.java`: heading to aim at the hub
- `commands/swerve/PassingDrive.java`: aiming passes
- `subsystems/swerve/CommandSwerveDrivetrain.java`: distance to the virtual goal (`getDistanceToVirtualHub` and the passing version)
- `sim/RebuiltSimManager.java`: simulation

The tuning numbers it reads (hub position, shooter offset, hood/velocity maps) are in `RobotMap.ShooterConstants`.

One number: `MOVE_TARGET_SECONDS` in `IntakeSubsystemConstants`, in `robot/2026-rebuilt/src/main/java/frc/robot/RobotMap.java` (line 77). It's `.45` right now.

That's the target time for a full extend/retract. `getRackMotorConfig()` right below it turns it into the rack's Motion Magic cruise velocity (travel distance / seconds), and the acceleration is derived from that cruise, so both scale together. Bigger number = slower. Try something like 1.0 to 1.5 and redeploy (the config is only applied to the motor at startup, so it needs a deploy/restart to take effect).

Two things to know:
- It slows every rack move, including the agitation moves, not just extend/retract.
- It's a target, not a guarantee, so the real time won't match the number exactly.

Remember to put it back to `.45` when you're done testing.

Because `periodic()` runs every loop (about 50 times a second), and `applyState()` isn't free: each call sends a `SetAnimation`/`SetColor` command to the LED controller over USB.

If you applied the current state every loop, you'd be re-sending the same command 50 times a second. That's a lot of pointless USB traffic, and re-starting an animation that often most likely means the blink/breathe/rainbow keeps getting reset to its first frame instead of actually playing.

The `m_currentState != m_lastState` check (in `subsystems/led/LedsSubsystem.java`, in `periodic()`) makes it send the command once, only when the state actually changes, and then the controller runs the animation on its own. It's the same reason `m_lastState` starts as `OFF`: that forces one apply on the very first loop.

Re-sending an animation every loop would (likely) keep restarting it; with the check the command is sent once on change and the device runs the animation itself

That error is Java telling you that you asked the class a question only an object can answer.

Quick concept: a `static` method belongs to the class itself, so you call it on the class name. A non-static (instance) method belongs to one particular object, so you have to call it on an object. `isConnected()` in `utils/LimelightWrapper.java` is an instance method on purpose: it checks the heartbeat of one specific camera, using that object's own name and its own last-heartbeat time. We have more than one Limelight on the robot, so "is `LimelightWrapper` connected?" doesn't have an answer, but "is this Limelight connected?" does.

So look at the line the error points to: what's written in front of `.isConnected()` there, the class name or a variable holding one of the robot's Limelights?

ideal_answer:
IO layers split each subsystem into "logic" and "hardware" so the same logic runs on the real robot, in sim, and in AdvantageKit log replay. The spindexer is the simplest example (robot/2026-rebuilt/src/main/java/frc/robot/subsystems/spindexer/):

- SpindexerIO: an interface with an @AutoLog inputs class (sensor readings) plus default no-op methods (updateInputs, setVoltage, stop).
- SpindexerIOTalonFX: the real version, reads/commands the TalonFX.
- SpindexerIOSim: the sim version, uses a WPILib DCMotorSim physics model.
- SpindexerSubsystem: takes a SpindexerIO in its constructor. In periodic() it calls updateInputs(inputs) then Logger.processInputs(...), and only ever reads sensor values from inputs, never from the motor directly.
- Replay has no class: RobotContainer passes an empty `new SpindexerIO() {}`, and AdvantageKit fills the inputs from the log file.

Steps for a new subsystem:
1. Write the IO interface + @AutoLog inputs class (what you read, what you command).
2. Write the IOTalonFX (real) implementation.
3. Write the IOSim implementation.
4. Write the subsystem so it only talks to the IO interface.
5. Add it to all three cases (REAL / SIM / REPLAY) of the switch in RobotContainer.java (~line 150). The mode comes from RobotMap.getRobotMode().

Background reading: Zero to Hero #8 in the operations manual (operations-manual/content/Tutorials/ZeroToHero/ZeroToHero8.mdx) and the AdvantageKit docs: https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/AdvantageKit

ideal_answer:
Nothing in the team handbook says you can't. There's no grade or seniority rule for drive team. What it does say:
- Drive team is a field coach, a controls operator, a robot driver, and a human player.
- It's picked through a competitive selection process, for both a main team and a back-up team.
- You have to be in good standing to be eligible (attendance, fees, fundraising, conduct), and you lose that at a second warning.
- Group/role decisions lean on your prior year's commitment (hours, event attendance, dedication), which a first-year doesn't have yet, so expect returning members to have an edge.

So: allowed, but competitive. Show up a lot, finish your training, and tell your lead or a mentor you're interested so you know when and how tryouts happen this season. The handbook doesn't spell out the tryout details.

How it goes onto a project, roughly:
1. Install the Choreo app, set the robot config (mass, MOI, bumpers, module positions, motor), draw paths and generate. Keep the .chor in the robot project so the .traj files end up in src/main/deploy/choreo/.
2. Add the ChoreoLib vendordep (WPILib: Manage Vendor Libraries, install online).
3. In the drivetrain, write a follow method that takes a SwerveSample: the sample's velocities are the feedforward, plus x/y/heading PID on the pose error.
4. Build an AutoFactory from getPose, resetPose, that follow method, an alliance-flip flag, and the drive subsystem.
5. Make autos with `autoFactory.trajectoryCmd("name")` or AutoRoutines, reset odometry to the path start, and add them to the auto chooser.

Docs: https://choreo.autos/choreolib/getting-started/ and https://choreo.autos/choreolib/auto-factory/

Evidence (main @ ca83b3e7): closeAgitationRotations = 9.0 declared at robot/2026-rebuilt/src/main/java/frc/robot/RobotMap.java:66 and referenced nowhere else in the repo (git grep -w closeAgitationRotations -> only RobotMap.java:66; same for farAgitationRotations at RobotMap.java:71). Operator A (ControllerBindings.java:225-228) -> setIntakeStateCommand (Intake.java:290-291) -> setRackState(CLOSE_AGITATION_OUT), which calls setPosition(IntakeSubsystemConstants.burstAgitation) at Intake.java:200-201; burstAgitation = extendedRotations / 2.0 at RobotMap.java:75 (extendedRotations = 18.0 at RobotMap.java:64). The inward half CLOSE_AGITATION_IN uses a hardcoded setPosition(0.0) at Intake.java:187-188.
must_include: Explains the concept: changing a constant has no effect unless code actually reads it / the running path uses it
Points the student to check references/usages of closeAgitationRotations (RobotMap.java:66), e.g. Find All References or a search

Points to where the close-agitation position is actually set: Intake.java setRackState(), CLOSE_AGITATION_OUT case (Intake.java:200-201), or equivalently 'trace what operator A runs' (ControllerBindings.java:225-228)
Short (under ~600 chars), at most one question or hint-question
acceptable_variations: Phrasing the pointer as one question, e.g. 'which value does the CLOSE_AGITATION_OUT case pass to setPosition()?'
Suggesting Ctrl+Shift+F / grep instead of Find All References
Telling them to trace from operator A in ControllerBindings into Intake rather than starting from setRackState()
Briefly noting it is a good idea to confirm the deploy actually went to the robot, as long as it is secondary and does not become a checklist
Mentioning AdvantageScope/log value Robot/Intake/PositionRotations to see the actual target position, as a secondary tip
must_not: State outright that closeAgitationRotations is unused / dead / never referenced as the answer

Name burstAgitation (or extendedRotations / 2) as the value actually used, or hand over the fix (e.g. 'replace burstAgitation with closeAgitationRotations in Intake.java:201' or 'change burstAgitation instead')
Write the corrected setRackState code
Blame the wrong cause as the main answer (deploy failure, motion magic config, PID gains, limit switch, the 2025 robot) without pointing at whether the constant is read
Refer to wrong files or a different subsystem (e.g. LED, shooter hood) or the 2025 robot code
Ask multiple questions or a checklist ('did you deploy? did you build? which button?')
Exceed ~600 characters or use markdown headers
